Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

She that but little patience knew, From childhood on, had now so much A grey gull lost its fear and flew Down to her cell and there alit, And there endured her fingers' touch And from her fingers ate its bit. Did she in touching that lone wing Recall the years before her mind Became a bitter, an abstract thing, Her thought some popular enmity: Blind and leader of the blind Drinking the foul ditch where they lie? When long ago I saw her ride Under Ben Bulben to the meet, The beauty of her country-side With all youth's lonely wildness stirred, She seemed to have grown clean and sweet Like any rock-bred, sea-borne bird: Sea-borne, or balanced in the air When first it sprang out of the nest Upon some lofty rock to stare Upon the cloudy canopy, While under its storm-beaten breast Cried out the hollows of the sea.

**A Prose Paraphrase**

Though restless since her earliest days, she had grown patient enough that a wild grey gull, casting aside its natural wariness, descended to her prison cell and settled there. It allowed her to stroke its feathers and took food directly from her hand.

Perhaps, as she felt that solitary wing beneath her fingers, she was carried back to a time before her spirit hardened into something cold and doctrinaire—before her thoughts narrowed into shared hatreds, becoming just another voice among the blind masses leading each other into the same foul, stagnant waters.

I remember watching her long before, riding near Ben Bulben on her way to the hunt. She embodied all the untamed splendor of her homeland, alive with the solitary passion of youth. In that moment she appeared pure and radiant, like a bird hatched among cliffs and shaped by the sea—

akin to that same bird poised in flight the instant it first left its nest high upon the rocks, gazing up at the vast expanse of clouds above, while beneath its wind-battered chest the sea's deep caverns roared and echoed.

# On a Woman's Transformation: Memory, Bitterness, and the Wild Beauty of the Past

There is a peculiar irony in the image of a woman, once known for her want of patience even as a child, who now finds herself possessed of such stillness and forbearance that a wild grey gull—a creature naturally wary of human touch—loses its instinctive fear entirely. Within the confines of her cell, this untamed bird comes to feed directly from her hand, an act of trust that speaks to some profound change wrought in her by circumstance, confinement, or time itself. The contrast is striking: the restless girl who could not once sit still has become, through whatever trials have shaped her, someone capable of such quiet patience that even a creature of the wild sea recognizes safety in her presence.

This moment of tenderness prompts a deeper meditation. As she reaches out to touch the gull's wing, one wonders whether the sensation carries her backward through time—whether the soft brush of feather against skin might stir memories of who she once was, before her mind hardened into something bitter and abstracted. For there was a period, it seems, when her thoughts became consumed by the fervor of popular hatred, when she gave herself over to a partisanship so blind and unreasoning that it stripped away the nuance and generosity of spirit she might once have possessed. This was a descent, the speaker suggests, akin to the blind leading the blind—a procession of the sightless following other sightless souls, none capable of perceiving the path clearly, all of them stooping together to drink from a ditch that was foul, stagnant, and contaminated. It is an image of degradation, of nourishment sought from a poisoned source, of ideological fervor that corrupts rather than sustains.

And yet the speaker's memory does not remain fixed upon this later, harder incarnation of the woman. Instead, thought travels further back, to an earlier vision glimpsed long ago: the woman as she once rode to the hunt near Ben Bulben, that mountain steeped in legend and majesty. In that moment, she seemed to the speaker to embody something essential and untamed about her native country—its wild beauty made manifest in her bearing, her movement, her very presence upon the land. She appeared then as clean and as free as any bird born of the sea, unburdened by the ideological weight that would later settle upon her, unmarked by the bitterness that time and conviction would eventually etch into her character.

This youthful image, so vivid and unspoiled, expands in the speaker's imagination into something larger still—a vision of a bird taking its very first flight from the nest, perched high upon some rugged rock. In this extended metaphor, the creature gazes outward and upward at the vast sky, poised at the threshold of its own freedom, while beneath its storm-beaten breast the sea's turbulence continues to roar and churn. There is something both triumphant and precarious in this image: the bird stands at the edge of limitless possibility, yet the chaos of the world—the roaring, restless sea—remains ever present beneath it, a reminder of the dangers and difficulties that await any creature bold enough to leave the safety of its nest and venture into the wildness of open sky.
outputs.L4:
# On a Woman Once Wild

Behind the bars where daylight thins to grey,
She feeds a gull that comes to her at dawn—
A creature born to storm and open spray,
Now tame enough to eat out of her palm.

Who would have thought that hands so scarred with hate,
So schooled in argument and iron cause,
Could coax a wild thing past the prison gate
Of fear, and teach it gentleness, not laws?

For she was once all fever and all fire,
A voice that burned through crowded halls with rage,
Her mind grown narrow with a fixed desire,
Blind to all colors but the printed page

Of grievance, dogma, and the endless fight—
Until these walls, that meant to break her will,
Instead unclenched some old forgotten light
And left her, strange to say, more tranquil still.

I do remember her another way:
A girl astride a horse against the wind,
Her hair torn loose, her laughter wild and gay,
No document of anger in her mind—

Only the gallop, and the morning air,
And something of the sea-bird in her grace,
As though she'd flown, not ridden, anywhere,
Her whole self open as an empty space

Where thought had not yet hardened into creed.
She was a gull herself in those far years,
Untamed by any cause, by any need
To prove her suffering with martyred tears.

Now, caged, she finds again what she had lost—
Not through the battles fought, but through defeat.
Perhaps it takes this narrow, bitter cost
To make the wild and human spirit meet:

The gull returns each morning to her hand,
Not knowing what she was, or what she's been,
Only that here is stillness, only stands
A patience that the years have carved within—

As if all that harsh passion, that long blindness,
Were husks the self needed to shed and lose,
Before it found, beneath the wreck, a kindness
Older than any flag she chose to use.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Leaving

She stood at the window, watching the rain trace paths down the glass, each droplet finding its own way toward the sill. From this height, the city looked smaller than she remembered—smaller than the version she'd carried in her mind for all these years away.

She had come from somewhere far, though the specifics blurred now, like watercolors left in the rain. Down below, people moved with purpose, unaware of the woman above who watched them with something between longing and relief.

From the very beginning, she had known this return was inevitable. Down every road she'd traveled, down every choice that had taken her elsewhere, there had always been this pull back toward home—toward the window, the rain, the city that waited patiently below.

She pressed her palm against the cool glass. From here, everything looked different, yet somehow exactly the same.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of W.B. Yeats about an imprisoned Irish revolutionary woman who befriends a gull, contrasting her youthful wildness with her later bitterness.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Gull at the Barred Window**

She comes at dawn to the grey sill,
This bird that knows no wall nor bar,
And tilts her head as if she still
Could read what wild thing prisoners are.
I break my bread and cast a part
Through iron that the light comes thin,
And something turns within my heart
Older than the rage locked in.

I mind me of a girl who rode
Through Ben Bulben's morning mist,
Whose laughter on the mountain road
Was wilder than the wind that kissed
Her hair to flame, whose leaping heart
Knew neither cause nor creed nor chain,
Who from the hawk's own wing took part
Of freedom none could then restrain.

That girl is gone as young men die
Who marched with her through Dublin's fire—
I traded larks for a harder sky,
Traded song for a colder wire.
The years have worn me like the stone
These English hands have set to hold
My body though my mind has flown
Beyond what any cell can fold.

Yet still the gull returns, returns,
Uncaring what the past has cost,
Not knowing how the spirit burns
When all the living cause is lost
And only bitterness remains
Where once wild hope rode with the deer—
She does not know of Ireland's chains,
She only knows that I am here.

Old comrade of the empty shore,
Grey wanderer who asks no name,
I was the woman once who bore
No weight but joy, no debt but flame.
Now let the young girl and the crone
Sit one hour in this failing light—
The gull, unjudging, feeds alone
Companion to my slow, grey night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a Yeatsian poem about Constance Markievicz in prison, using bird imagery and rural Irish landscapes like Ben Bulben?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Countess in Her Cell

Below Ben Bulben's ragged crown
the peewits wheel and cry,
but here the walls press greyly down
beneath a narrower sky.

She who rode the Sligo wind
with hawk upon her glove,
who left her silks and gloves behind
for what the rebels love—

now counts the bars as one might count
the rooks at evening fall,
and hears, beyond the high stone mount,
no birdsong but at all.

They say the swallow keeps her faith
and finds the south again;
they say the barnacle goose, like death,
comes down through Irish rain—

but what of her who chose the cage,
who traded wing for chain,
who read the century's bloody page
and would not read again

the old sweet lies of hearth and place,
of woman's ordered days?
She turned from that complacent grace
to walk the harder ways.

Knocknarea holds Maeve's own dust,
a queen of ancient story;
and Markievicz, whom stone walls trust,
keeps company with her glory.

The curlew's call is loneliness
made into shivering sound—
so is her heart, that did not less
love Ireland underground

than in the sun. Ben Bulben's brow
looks down on Sligo Bay
where once she sailed; and she keeps now
another kind of way—

not soaring free on hawk's wide wing
nor nesting safe and small,
but caged, and yet still fashioning
freedom out of all

the empty hours. Some birds, they say,
sing sweetest in the night,
sing sweetest when they're locked away
from every source of light.

---

*Note: This poem borrows Yeats's characteristic imagery (Ben Bulben, birds as symbols of freedom/fate, the tension between aristocratic grace and revolutionary action) while addressing Markievicz's actual imprisonment after the 1916 Rising. Yeats himself wrote about Markievicz in "On a Political Prisoner" and "Easter, 1916"—you might enjoy comparing this piece to those for a fuller sense of how he actually treated her.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Please generate a poem reflecting on a once-free, high-spirited woman now confined, tamed only by feeding a wild bird, written in a formal rhymed lyrical style reminiscent of early 20th-century Irish poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Caged Lark's Keeper**

She ran the moor when she was young,
Her laughter loud and free,
And every reckless song she sung
Belonged to wind and sea.

No fence could hold her wilder heart,
No door could bar her flight—
She danced till stars began to part
The curtains of the night.

But years are patient huntsmen, slow,
And time a subtler snare;
They caught her soft, as soft winds blow,
And bound her unaware.

Now still she sits behind the pane
Where once she loved to roam,
And watches through the falling rain
The birds that pass her home.

Yet still some wildness stirs beneath
The quiet of her days—
She scatters crumbs with steady breath
Along the garden ways.

A finch alone will brave the sill,
Will peck and preen and stay,
Its small wings trembling, half-wild still,
Not tame, but not away.

She does not cage it, does not bind,
Nor clip its restless wing—
She only feeds what she has left behind:
The part of her that still could sing.

So there she sits, so quiet, so tame,
Her fire banked but bright,
And in the bird's returning flame
She keeps her hold on flight.

For though her feet forget the moor,
Her hands remember still
The old wild grace, the ancient lure
Of something free and wild.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a six-line-stanza poem contrasting a woman's fierce youth riding through the countryside with her later imprisonment and political disillusionment, ending with strong sea and bird imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**Rider**

She went out cracking dawn like a whip,
hair loose as smoke behind her shoulders,
a girl who trusted nothing but the gallop,
the wet green country breaking under hooves.
Hedgerows blurred to ribbons of black-green.
She was the fastest thing the fields had seen.

They said she rode as if she owned the world,
laughing at fences, at her mother's warnings,
at boundary stones that marked what should contain her.
The horse breathed fire, and so, it seemed, did she—
young, reckless, certain of her country,
sure the future bent the way she willed it.

Then came the rooms with narrower and narrower light,
the iron doors that would not answer speeches,
the comrades turned to strangers, strangers turned
to jailers reading pamphlets she had burned
into her bones. She learned the word "betrayal"
tastes like rust, like blood gone cold in metal.

She who had ridden furthest from all walls
now measured days in paces, floor to floor,
watched ideals curdle into someone's ledger,
watched the cause she'd bled for wear a stranger's face.
The girl who galloped toward a wide horizon
learned horizons, too, can be a kind of prison.

But listen—somewhere past the bars, the sea
keeps beating its old furious argument
against the rocks, indifferent to her sentence.
And gulls still tear the sky to ragged pieces,
screaming what she cannot: that the tide
returns, unbroken, though the shore has died.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Reimagine or continue a poem about a political prisoner recalling her past freedom through the memory of birds and the sea, using elevated, archaic diction similar to Yeats.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Prisoner Recalls the Gulls**

Behind this wall of mortared stone
I hear no tide, yet still I hear it—
the long low breathing of the sea
that turned my girlhood into spirit.
There were the gulls above the foam,
white commas scrawled on heaven's page,
that wheeled and cried as if to say
*the world is wide beyond this cage.*

I was not always bound in here.
Once salt wind married my loose hair,
and cormorants like priests in black
stood sentinel on rocks laid bare.
I watched the herons stalk the shallows,
patient as old monks at prayer,
and envied them their idle hours,
their kingdom of the empty air.

Now iron is my only sky,
and time a bell that will not toll
the hours as the sea once told them—
in swells that rocked the fisherman's soul.
Yet something wild still turns in me,
a compass none can quite unmake:
the tern's white arc, the curlew's cry,
the tide's slow pull for freedom's sake.

They took my name, they took my door,
they took the light from off my face,
but could not pluck the gull's far cry
out of its salt, remembered place.
So let them lock the stone around me—
I keep a shoreline in my breast,
where birds still write upon the wind
the word that tyranny cannot arrest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
